While designs vary for both microphones and speakers, the actual conversion process remains fundamentally the same.
The cone movement disrupts the air on either side of the cone and creates sound waves.
This, in turn, drives the voice coil and cone in or out depending on direction of current flow.
When current flows through the voice coil, a magnetic field is induced that interacts with the magnetic field of the permanent magnet.
The AF (Audio Frequency) from the amplifier is put across the inputs of a speaker which are actually opposite ends of a voice coil.
A loudspeaker contains essentially the same elements in, basically, the same order. The cone and diaphragm have the same function.
This conversion process is reversed when audio frequency is turned into sound.
The audio frequencies created by the induced energy are the intelligence that modulates the radio frequency transmitted into the air and picked up by receivers.
As the diaphragm reacts to the changes in air pressure, the coil moves back and forth through the flux lines of the magnetic field, including an electromotive force in the coil.
The diaphragm is connected to a coil of fine wire called a "voice coil". This coil is positioned within a magnetic field.
Here they collide with a sensitive diaphragm designed to respond to even slight variations in air pressure.
Consider a local broadcast station. When an announcer speaks into a microphone, the sound waves are projected into the sound receptor section.
Because the human ear is incapable of detecting radio waves, they must first be converted to sound waves. The reverse process must be used before a transmission takes place.
In most cases, information being transmitted and received through a communication system will be in the range of audio frequencies.

While this may appear to be a matter of designing high gain amplifier stages, noise must be factored into the equation. If the signal is amplified, so is the noise. Conversely, noise may not be reduced without an equal reduction of signal.
A receiver's sensitivity lies in its ability to lock onto a weak signal and correctly reproduce the intended information.

An AM station may be broadcasting as 620 kHz, while elsewhere another station may be broadcasting at 630 kHz. A receiver must be able to reject neighboring frequencies while tuning to the desired frequency.
AM broadcast stations are able to cover large geographical areas.
Selectivity is a receiver's ability to tune to a specific frequency while rejecting others.
From the perspective of the final audible product, there is a fine line between noise and distortion.

Distortion is the degradation of a signal, commonly resulting from overdriven amplifiers, where the peaks of the waveform are clipped or flattened. This results in the loss of upper and lower frequencies.
Because noise is unpredictable, it is difficult to design circuitry that can completely eliminate noise.
Band specific filters greatly assist in eliminating much of the noise, both internal and external.

Internal noise (sometimes called Johnson Noise) is generated by all the components of the system and, for the most part, is accumulative. That is, noise generated in one stage is amplified in the next.

Galactic noise is commonly caused by sunspots, and may be strong enough to completely blank out normal reception. This is particularly true in communication systems like cable TV, that use satellites.
Noises generated outside our atmosphere are considered galactic.
Atmospheric noises are predominantly caused by lightning...

Externally speaking, noise may be derived from man-made, atmospheric and galactic sources. Man-made noises, like those in an industrial environment, often decrease frequency. Common culprits are engine ignition systems and high-voltage power lines.

Understanding both the nature and origins of noise is necessary from a technician's perspective with regard to system alignment or any other maintenance operation.

In any communication system, noise is created by both external and internal sources. Since there isn't any known way to isolate the system from the problem of noise, limiting it is the best that can be achieved.

Once the signal is received, the AM detector and filter network will eliminate all but the original audio signal. This process of extracting the intelligence from the carrier frequency is known as demodulation.

The audio signal is replicated on the positive side of the carrier, while on the negative side of the carrier, it is 180 degrees out of phase. Some receivers use the positive side of the carrier while others use the negative side.

By using modulation, the parameters change by a large factor. If the 10 kHz signal was being "carried" by a 90 MHz signal, the wavelength is 10.9 feet. Using a quarter-wave antenna, the length need only be 2.06 feet long.
Still, using the parameters from the previous calculation, the antenna could only be reduced to 2.32 miles long. This would still be a problem if you wanted to drive a car with a radio.
While antenna length is a problem, through the use of image frequencies and other antenna theory, 1/2, 1/4 and 1/8 wave antennas may be utilized.

Ideally, an antenna should be as long as the frequency it is receiving. Using a frequency somewhere in the middle of the human hearing spectra, (16Hz to 16 kHz), the wavelength or antenna length for a 10 kHz frequency would be 18.6 miles long!
The process of using an audio signal to modulate the frequency of a higher "carrier signal" was developed primarily to reduce the necessity for excessively long antennas.

One way of thinking about modulation is as the process of altering some characteristic of a frequency (the carrier) as a direct response of another signal. In the case of AM, FM, CB, NBFM or SSB, the audio signal.
The transmission and reception (through a wireless medium) of any information requires superimposing the waveform onto an RF carrier. This "modulates" the carrier signal.

As mentioned, the first requirement for a communications system is to have information or some form of intelligence to be conveyed. This might be in the form of voice, music, or coded signal. In communications, the terms "information", "intelligence", and "data" are synonymous.

For example, AM broadcasts use 535 to 1605 kHz, while FM broadcasts are assigned at 88 to 108 MHz. Without this assignment, the airwaves would become a whirlpool of sound, mostly unintelligible, overlapping one another.
Within the radio frequency range, certain bands have been assigned for particular applications.
The most commonly used radio frequencies (RF) range from
30 kHz to 30 GHz. Some even lower frequencies are used in sonar and submarine communications, while some higher frequencies are used in weather radar and secure government communications.
The waves that can be detected by the human ear (approximately 16Hz to 16 kHz) are considered audio frequencies (AF). Before we can hear these frequencies they must first be converted to sound waves.
The frequency spectrum exists all around us in the form of electromagnetic waves that range in the frequency of 1 Hz on up to many Gigahertz.
